prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Home, Geometry, Old

outputs.L1:
I was someone’s honors student once—a sticker, a star. I aced Home Ec and Geometry; I learned to stab a fork and steer my mother’s car. Old enough to work, I refreshed the salad bar at Steak & Ale, scarcity a line I couldn’t fail. During the summers between university years, I interned at AT&T through the minority-outreach program they called INROADS. My boss, Vicki, had two roommates, whom she called simply The Gays, crashing on her floor. That was before I was gay—I won’t try to say it with a straight face. As if anyone really cares. I care.

What I’m trying to say is that all of this prepared me for these squat, blinking office accessories. The dry drinking after the accidental reply-all. By now, there’s a lot to lose. Little by little, I have become so careful: no talk of politics or orientation. I let them say he’s “a homosexual” without an arch correction.

At a fondue buffet in Zurich, our dumbfounded senior group director—after I let slip, damn it, my trip with a twenty-year-old—inquired, “They’re always over seventeen, right?” I told her, “Of course. God, yes,” and, seething, smiled—which I’m famous for. I didn’t want to scare her. But I tell you, I’m keeping score.

E-mail is no more than a suicide I’d like to please recall. Note my suicide. I’m paid to multitask, to scramble the life out of fun. Monday, I will ask—every dash a loaded gun, every comma a knife—you to bury the black-box file.
outputs.L2:
Once, I was a teacher’s prized pupil—the kid rewarded with gold stars and stickers. I earned top marks in Home Economics and Geometry, mastered proper fork use, and learned to drive my mother’s car. When I became old enough for a job, I restocked the salad bar at Steak & Ale, where an empty tray was a standard I dared not miss. During summer breaks from university, I worked at AT&T through Inroads, the minority internship program. My supervisor, Vicki, shared her place with two men who slept on her floor and whom she referred to only as “The Gays.” This happened before I understood myself as gay—though I cannot make that claim convincingly. Maybe nobody else is concerned, but I am.

My point is that every one of those experiences trained me for a life among these square, flickering objects on an office desk: the tense, sober drinks that follow an unintended reply-all. At this stage, I have too much at stake. Gradually, caution has taken over. I avoid discussing politics or sexual orientation. When coworkers describe someone as “a homosexual,” I resist offering a pointed correction.

At a fondue spread in Zurich, I mistakenly mentioned traveling with a twenty-year-old. Our astonished senior group director then asked whether my companions were always older than seventeen. Furious but smiling—the expression I am known for—I assured her that, yes, of course they were. I did not want to frighten her. Still, believe me, I remember every offense.

An email is merely a form of self-destruction that I wish could be retrieved. Pay attention to my own act of erasure. My salary depends on juggling tasks and stripping the pleasure from everything. On Monday, I will ask you—while each dash feels like a cocked firearm and every comma like a blade—to dispose of the black-box file.
outputs.L3:
The speaker recalls being a high-achieving student whose strong academic performance was complemented by early work experience in restaurants and at AT&T. These formative experiences taught the speaker discipline, professionalism, and how to navigate demanding environments. They also served as preparation for a corporate office culture characterized by caution, stress, and an acute awareness of how every action might be interpreted.

Within this workplace, the speaker carefully conceals or minimizes discussions of sexual orientation. This restraint is presented as a strategy for avoiding conflict and protecting the professional success they have worked hard to achieve. Rather than feeling free to speak openly about personal relationships, the speaker continually weighs the possible consequences of disclosure.

That tension becomes especially visible when a senior colleague asks an offensive question about the speaker’s younger partner. Although the remark provokes intense anger, the speaker suppresses any outward reaction and responds with a controlled smile. The moment illustrates the emotional labor required to remain composed in the face of prejudice, particularly when confronting someone with greater institutional power.

The speaker extends this sense of danger to everyday workplace communication. Email, word choice, and even punctuation seem potentially hazardous because each detail can be misunderstood, judged, or used against the sender. As a result, communication becomes an exercise in constant self-monitoring rather than genuine connection. The speaker suggests that this relentless caution has drained language of spontaneity, pleasure, and life, leaving behind a sterile form of professionalism shaped by fear.
outputs.L4:
The speaker recounts a life shaped by achievement, concealment, and the constant need to anticipate other people’s prejudice. He begins with his youth, presenting himself as ambitious, disciplined, and accustomed to succeeding. Yet these early accomplishments do not protect him from the anxiety attached to his sexuality. As he enters professional life, he learns to divide his public identity from his private one, becoming increasingly guarded about what he says, how he behaves, and what personal details he allows colleagues to see. His success therefore carries an emotional price: advancement depends not only on competence but also on his ability to monitor himself.

Autobiographical episodes make this conflict concrete. Rather than discussing discrimination only in abstract terms, the speaker shows how it operates in ordinary interactions, casual remarks, and workplace expectations. He describes an environment in which heterosexuality is treated as the unquestioned norm, while any disclosure of gay identity risks changing how others perceive him. Irony sharpens this critique. The workplace may claim to value honesty, individuality, and open communication, but it implicitly rewards silence and conformity. The speaker is expected to be authentic enough to appear personable, yet not so authentic that his identity makes others uncomfortable.

His language becomes especially revealing when he describes professional communication through violent metaphors. Emails, meetings, and minor verbal choices are imagined as weapons, traps, or acts of self-destruction. This imagery conveys how threatening even routine office life has become. A message written in frustration might damage his reputation; an incautious disclosure might endanger his career; a misplaced word or punctuation mark might be interpreted as aggression. What should be harmless communication is transformed into a potentially fatal professional act.

The focus on email and punctuation also demonstrates how deeply self-censorship has entered the speaker’s mind. He does not merely revise his ideas for clarity. He scrutinizes tone, removes signs of emotion, and suppresses any anger that might confirm stereotypes or make him seem difficult. Every sentence must be professionally safe. In this context, punctuation becomes symbolic: an exclamation mark, a full stop, or an emphatic phrase can appear dangerous because it may expose feelings he has spent years controlling. The metaphor of “professional suicide” captures the disproportionate consequences he fears from even a small mistake.

By the end, the speaker’s caution is shown not as a personality trait but as the result of accumulated experience. Years of concealment have taught him that openness can be punished and that anger, however justified, must remain hidden. His restrained voice therefore contains a powerful tension. Beneath the humor and irony lies resentment at a culture that demands constant emotional discipline from those who do not fit its assumptions.

Ultimately, the account exposes the psychological cost of surviving in an intolerant workplace. The speaker may remain outwardly successful, composed, and articulate, but that composure depends on continual vigilance. He must edit not only his emails but also his identity, relationships, and emotional responses. Through autobiography, irony, and violent imagery, he reveals that prejudice does more than limit professional opportunity: it forces individuals to treat self-expression as a threat and silence as a condition of employment.

The old house stood at the end of a narrow road, its shape defined by quiet geometry: square windows, triangular gables, and a round brass handle on the front door. Time had softened its angles, but it still felt balanced and familiar.

Inside, every room held a pattern. Floorboards ran in parallel lines, faded tiles formed small diamonds, and the staircase curved gently toward the upper floor. These simple shapes gave order to years of memories.

It was more than an old building. It was home—a place where geometry and history met, creating a space that felt steady, warm, and timeless.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary prose poem in the voice of a gay office worker reflecting on his path from honors student and restaurant employee to corporate life, using dark humor, internal rhyme, and anxiety about email, identity, and self-censorship.
counterfactuals.output:
My résumé begins with Latin honors and ends with “proficient in Outlook,” which is also how civilizations decline. Once, I underlined the word *liminal* in three colors. Once, I could explain the allegory of the cave without mentioning fluorescent lighting. Then came the restaurant: black apron, back ache, smile filed sharp as a shiv. I learned to carry six plates and one private panic, to call strangers “folks,” to flirt for tips while pretending my wrist had no biography. The kitchen called me professor; the dining room called me sweetheart; the manager called me in on Sunday.

Now I work where the carpet is the color of surrender. My job is to move language from one rectangle to another without letting it become legally interesting. I draft, redraft, laugh at nothing. Every email begins *Hi* and ends *Best*, a tiny pageant in which I am neither. Before I hit Send, I audit myself: Is this clear? Is this queer? Is the exclamation point too eager, too fragrant? I delete *just*, then add it back, then delete the sentence, then briefly consider deleting my identity from the shared drive.

The office knows I have a husband because benefits demanded evidence. Love enters corporate life through a drop-down menu. At happy hour, someone asks what my wife does, and I say, “He’s in healthcare,” with the calm of a bomb technician clipping the correct cliché. Everyone apologizes beautifully. We sip, we pivot, we praise the hummus. Inclusion is a webinar you can watch later, though later never comes.

Sometimes I miss the restaurant, where disaster had heat and a ticket number. A steak could be wrong in a way an email cannot: visibly, forgivably, medium-rarely. Here, mistakes reproduce by reply-all. At 2:13 a.m. I wake convinced I attached the salary spreadsheet, the private complaint, my whole soft underbelly named FINAL_v7. I reach for my phone like a priest for a bell. No catastrophe—only a calendar reminder titled “Be Yourself: Employee Wellness Session.”

I was an honors student because praise felt like proof. I was a server because rent felt like rent. I am corporate because dental work is expensive and death, apparently, is not. Still, beneath the blue-light pallor, some former self keeps raising his hand. He knows the answer. He also knows not to answer too quickly. He has learned the office catechism: circle back, take this offline, bring your whole self to work—but trim the whole self first, make it fit the file, the smile, the style guide. Then save. Then save as. Then, trembling slightly, Send.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a confessional free-verse poem that connects childhood achievement stickers, a Steak & Ale salad bar job, an AT&T minority internship, and an awkward corporate trip to Zurich. End with an ominous request to bury a “black-box file.”
counterfactuals.output:
I learned ambition in foil stars—  
red for reading,  
blue for arithmetic,  
gold when I smiled without being asked.

My mother pressed them into a shoebox  
as if praise could earn interest,  
as if one day I might cash them in  
at the bright counter of adulthood.

At Steak & Ale,  
I rebuilt the salad bar after every rush:  
ice under stainless steel,  
beets bleeding into cottage cheese,  
bacon bits scattered like small promotions.  
I wore a name tag and said  
Yes, ma’am, right away,  
while the sneeze guard held my face  
at a distance from the food.

Then AT&T called me  
a minority intern—  
three words clipped to my shirt  
more stubbornly than any star.  
I learned acronyms, handshakes,  
how to enter a conference room  
already grateful,  
how to laugh one beat after the vice president,  
how to make my difference  
sound like a deliverable.

Zurich came later:  
a corporate mercy in business class,  
my first passport stiff in my pocket.  
At dinner, no one knew where to put me.  
I mispronounced the wine,  
mistook the host’s wife for an interpreter,  
watched snow seal the windows  
while the table discussed global reach.

I said nothing about Steak & Ale,  
or the gold stars softening in their box,  
or how every ladder I climbed  
seemed to erase its lowest rung.

Back home, the expense report cleared.  
The photographs did not.  
In one, I am raising a glass  
with the frightened obedience  
of a child awaiting a sticker.

If anyone asks what happened in Zurich,  
tell them the system performed as designed.

And please—before the auditors arrive—  
bury the “black-box file.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a witty, unsettling dramatic monologue by a cautious middle-aged professional who hides his sexuality at work, smiles through homophobic remarks, and views every email as a potentially self-destructive act.
counterfactuals.output:
Every email is a small confession written under interrogation.

“Hi, Martin,” I type, and already I’ve revealed too much. *Hi* is warm. *Hello* is theatrical. *Dear* is practically a proposal. So I delete it and begin again.

“Martin—”

A dash. Efficient. Masculine. The punctuation of a man who owns at least one drill.

I’m fifty-one years old, Deputy Director of Compliance, and I have spent the better part of three decades ensuring that no sentence I write could be entered into evidence against me. Not legal evidence. Worse. Office evidence. The kind collected in kitchens, lifts, and private Teams chats titled “LEGENDS ONLY.”

At work, there are questions one answers and questions one survives.

“Do anything nice this weekend?”

“Yes, thanks.”

That is the answer. Not: *I drove to the coast with Daniel, and he fell asleep with his hand on my knee.* Not: *We argued about hydrangeas.* Not: *We have been together seventeen years and still pretend the spare bedroom is his whenever someone from the office comes over.*

“Yes, thanks. Quiet one.”

A quiet weekend. A quiet life. Quiet is such a useful little coffin.

The men at work like me. I have arranged this carefully. I know football scores, though not what they mean. I complain about parking. I say “the wife” in anecdotes that contain no wife and very little anecdote.

“The wife won’t let me,” I say, and they laugh.

No one asks what she won’t let me do.

Exist, perhaps.

At lunch, Graham from Procurement does impressions. Women, foreigners, gay men. His gay man has a loose wrist and an appetite for soft furnishings. The others laugh, then glance at me—not because they know, but because people always glance at the quietest person when ugliness enters a room.

So I smile.

Not broadly. Broadly would look eager. Not faintly. Faintly would look offended. I produce the precise smile of a senior professional acknowledging a minor fault in a spreadsheet.

“Careful,” I say. “HR will have you.”

This is considered wit.

Graham says, “Oh, come on, we’re all friends here.”

That sentence has buried more people than war.

Then my computer chimes.

An email from Daniel.

Subject: **Milk**

I stare at it as if it says **OUR SECRET HOMOSEXUAL HOUSEHOLD**.

I don’t open it immediately. That would suggest intimacy. I wait forty-seven seconds, during which I approve two invoices and consider dying.

*Can you pick up milk? Love you x*

There it is.

Love you.

A bomb in nine characters.

I look over my shoulder. Nobody is looking. Nobody ever is. This is the genius of fear: it doesn’t require an audience.

I delete the email. Then delete it from Deleted Items. Then wonder whether that looks suspicious to IT. Then restore it. Then move it into a folder called “Utilities.” Then worry that love, when misfiled, becomes fraud.

I reply:

*Fine.*

No greeting. No kiss.

A clean, hard, heterosexual word.

Daniel will read it in the kitchen, beneath the photograph of us in Lisbon that I keep facedown whenever colleagues visit. He will know what *Fine* means. It means *I love you too, but the company owns the server.*

He understands. That is one of the terrible things.

People imagine secrecy as a door you keep locked. It isn’t. It’s a house you live in. You dust it. You insure it. You replace the batteries in the smoke alarm. After a while, you stop noticing there are no windows.

At four, Martin sends a message:

*Quick one—can you come to my office?*

No message beginning “Quick one” has ever been quick, and no invitation to an office has ever improved a man’s pulse.

I walk there calmly. I have practiced calm. Calm is my principal transferable skill.

Martin closes the door.

He gestures for me to sit.

There is a printed email on his desk.

Printed.

An email in physical form is an execution notice.

He taps the paper.

My mouth goes dry. I see everything at once: Daniel packing a suitcase; Graham’s face rearranging itself into retrospect; my name becoming a punchline in rooms I used to enter freely.

Martin says, “You’ve put the wrong quarterly figure in the second paragraph.”

I look at the page.

He’s right.

A mistake.

An ordinary mistake.

I laugh too loudly.

Martin frowns. “Are you all right?”

“Yes,” I say.

Then, because panic makes daredevils of us, I add:

“Just relieved.”

“Relieved?”

I could tell him. There, in that bland room, under the framed certificate about inclusive leadership, I could simply say it. *Martin, I thought you’d discovered I buy milk for a man who loves me.*

Instead I smile.

“Relieved it’s only the figure.”

He nods. Of course. Compliance humour.

Back at my desk, I correct the email. I read it seven times. I remove an exclamation mark. Too emotional. I add “Regards.” Too cold. I change it to “Kind regards,” then back again.

My finger hovers over Send.

Such a tiny button.

Such a cheerful blue.

I think of Daniel at home, waiting for milk. I think of Graham’s loose wrist. I think of all the words I have swallowed becoming hard and bright inside me, like coins in a dead man’s stomach.

Then I click.

The email leaves.

For one beautiful second, nothing happens.

Then the computer chimes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental poem about code-switching and survival in corporate America. Include memories of Home Ec, Geometry, INROADS, an accidental reply-all, a fondue buffet, a younger boyfriend, and punctuation imagined as weapons.
counterfactuals.output:
**BUSINESS CASUAL / BODY ARMOR**

At 8:03 a.m. I badge in as  
**Good morning!**  
At 8:04 I become  
*per my last email,*  
a dialect with its teeth capped.

My mother’s voice waits in the stairwell:  
Don’t let them make you small.  
I say, Yes, ma’am.  
Then enter the meeting saying,  
Absolutely—happy to circle back.

Code-switch:  
verb, intransitive—  
to leave your real laugh in the car,  
engine running.

Home Ec taught me  
how to hem a skirt without drawing blood,  
how flour hides on black fabric,  
how a table should be set  
for people who may never invite you to eat.

Geometry taught me  
parallel lines do not meet,  
which sounded like policy:  
the executive track  
and me, advancing  
in the same bright building.

INROADS taught me another theorem:  
a foot in the door  
is still a foot under pressure.  
I learned the handshake, the name tag,  
the internship smile—  
learned to translate brilliance into  
*high potential,*  
hunger into  
*professional development.*

At 11:17, catastrophe:

I meant to tell one friend  
**this fondue buffet is a dairy-based hostage situation**

but clicked  
**REPLY ALL**

and suddenly Compliance, Finance,  
three VPs, the summer interns,  
and a man named Chip  
knew the truth about the cheese.

Silence arrived  
wearing a blazer.

Then laughter—  
first mine, too loud,  
then theirs, authorized.

At lunch I sharpen punctuation:

a comma: small sickle,  
semicolon: brass knuckles with a monocle,  
colon: twin warning shots,  
em dash: a blade slid across the sentence,  
parentheses: two shields  
I carry around what I really mean.

The exclamation point  
is a spear I decorate with cheer:

Great!  
Sounds good!  
No problem!  
I can take that on!

My younger boyfriend texts,  
**quit. come get tacos.**  
Lowercase, no armor.

He thinks survival means leaving.  
I think survival means direct deposit,  
dental, the annual bonus  
I pretend not to calculate in groceries.

He calls me *baby*  
while I revise myself for leadership:

less edge,  
more polish;  
less fire,  
more *visibility*;  
less Black, they never say,  
more *fit.*

At 4:46 someone compliments  
how articulate I am.

I become Home Ec again:  
fold the rage inward,  
pin it cleanly,  
press until no seam shows.

I become Geometry:  
an angle measuring  
how far I can bend  
without becoming another shape.

I become INROADS:  
a road built through  
what said there was no way through.

At 5:32 I badge out.

In the elevator mirror  
I return my vowels to their bodies.  
I text my mother in the language  
that knows me without credentials.

Outside, my boyfriend waits,  
young enough to believe  
every door deserves a kick.

Behind me, the office glows—  
a fondue pot left plugged in,  
everything expensive  
slowly becoming one indistinguishable thing.

Tomorrow I will come back  
with commas in my pockets,  
an em dash at my hip,  
my smile loaded—

Good morning!  
Good morning!  
Good morning!

which is not surrender.

It is the password  
and the weapon  
and the proof  
I survived the night.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a dense autobiographical prose poem with slant rhyme and wordplay, narrated by a queer Black corporate employee looking back on school, summer jobs, and workplace microaggressions while preparing to send a dangerous Monday email.
counterfactuals.output:
**SEND, 8:59 A.M.**

Monday loads its little gun in my outbox. I dress the bullet in Calibri, twelve-point, warm regards. All weekend I have revised the blast radius: *Per my previous—* no, too blade; *For clarity—* too courtroom; *I want to name a pattern—* there, a soft alarm with my name in it. I am Black enough to be read as weather, queer enough to know every closet has quarterly goals. At my desk I keep two mugs: WORLD’S OKAYEST EMPLOYEE and one my boyfriend painted, a crooked rainbow glazing the clay like oil on a puddle—pretty because something spilled.

School taught me early how to fold thunder into homework. In third grade, Mrs. Vale called me “articulate,” each syllable a gold star with a small white hook. By sixth, boys in the locker room had made my wrists a rumor. I learned the math of passing: subtract the swivel, divide the voice, carry the one secret home. Mama asked why I walked like an apology; I said my backpack was heavy. It was: Baldwin beside biology, shame beside Shakespeare, a lunchbox full of names I wouldn’t answer to but did. At graduation they praised my promise. I heard premises.

Summers, I worked wherever heat had a time clock. At the car wash I buffed rich men’s doors until my face came back warped and spotless. At the mall kiosk I sold cologne called *Dominion* to fathers who said, Be a man, young man, and I misted their wrists with forests no tree had agreed to. One July I filed invoices in an office cold as a bank’s heart; my supervisor touched my hair and said it was “fun,” as if my head were casual Friday. I smiled—my first unpaid internship in mercy. Every shift taught the same hymn with a different hum: yes, sir; no, ma’am; I can stay late; I don’t mind. Mind became mine’s quiet twin.

Now I badge into glass. The lobby swallows me whole and calls it inclusion. Upstairs, my ideas arrive twice: first in my mouth, then ten minutes later in Greg’s, wearing a tie and getting traction. Karen says I’m intimidating when I stop decorating my sentences with sorry. A vice president confuses me with Marcus—again—and laughs, “You know how it is.” I know how *it* is: a pronoun with plausible deniability. In the diversity photo, they place me center, a dark little lighthouse for a ship that will not turn. Someone asks what my partner “does,” then corrects *he* to *they* to *she* and finally to silence, where we all pretend the printer is fascinating.

Still, I have climbed—code-switch by switchback—until the view is mostly ceiling. My reviews say *leadership potential* and *tone*. Potential is a promissory note; tone is the interest. I mentor interns in stairwells, tell them which smiles are doors and which are décor. I tell them excellence is not armor, though I wore mine until it wore me: bright breastplate, tight breath. I tell them HR is not your mother. I do not tell them how often I call mine from the parking garage, lower my voice, and say, I’m fine, which slant-rhymes with survive.

The email waits. It contains dates, quotes, witnesses, the arithmetic of interruption. It says *bias* without blinking. It says *retaliation* and feels the room go thin. It says my name correctly. Dangerous, yes—not because it lies, but because truth in a corporation is an open flame near the org chart, because Monday prefers its Blackness brewed, not speaking; its queerness catered, not chaired. My cursor hovers like a small god over **Send**. In the black mirror of the sleeping screen, I see every boy I buried to become employable, every summer self smelling of wax, musk, toner, every polished no I swallowed whole.

At 8:59, the office blooms with pings. Good mornings perform their harmless harm. I straighten the rainbow mug beside the company one. I think of Mama, backpacks, Baldwin, premises and promise. I think: a trigger is also what makes a thing begin.

Then I press Monday where it hurts.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
